utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Thank you. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the technical booth, the interpreters; good morning, legal assistants, Registry, counsel for the Prosecution, counsel for the Defence; good morning to the accused. We will resume our hearing with the decision regarding the objection that was raised on Friday. The Chamber rejects the objection raised by the Defence last Friday. Nothing prevents the counsel from asking the witness if he or she has seen an accused at a particular date, although this date falls outside the time framework of the indictment. On the other hand, the Chamber is waiting for the conclusions of the Defence regarding the motion submitted by the Prosecutor concerning the consolidation of the indictment. The Prosecutor may respond to the Defence, and the Defence is also entitled to submit a reply to the response of the Prosecutor. The Chamber will, afterwards, render its decision thereof, and order, if necessary, a withdrawal of the files containing evidence which will be excluded by the decision. That concludes the Chamber's ruling, but I should like to tell you the following: I know that the Defence insists on receiving the B/C/S translation of the consolidated indictment. However, if it is only a matter of copying and pasting, as we have all agreed, maybe it is possible for the Defence to respond to the motion. We have the Prcac indictment as well. We also have the dates which are part of the motion for correction submitted by the Prosecutor, and as far as I know, it is very easy to correct the date, which was problematic, the 30th of August instead of 30th of July. I think that this is a technical matter which is rather easy to correct. However, I should like to hear the response to the motion as soon as possible. However, if the Defence insists on receiving the translation, we will slightly modify our last decision and say that upon the expiration of seven days after receiving the B/C/S translation, the Defence must respond. However, I still believe that it is possible for the Defence to respond before that, because nothing is significantly changed in respect of the translation that you already have. This is merely a suggestion by the Chamber, but this is also a right of the Defence. The Defence may request a translation, and once it receives the translation, it must respond within seven days. Having said that, I believe it is possible for us to resume the examination of Witness O, I believe, which we were conducting last Friday. Could the usher please bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're waiting for the witness, if I might, I would just like to advise the Court of slight changes in the witness order for this week, which unfortunately I failed to advise of you fry afternoon after the other issues that we took up. I did advise the Defence, however, and they have no objection. It relates to Witness AR, who was to come early this week. Given logistical issues for the witnesses already here, Witness AR has been moved off of the list for this week. The order now will be, after Witness O, it would be Mr. Mesanovic, then Mr. Mesan and, and then Witnesses F and

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right now it appears, based on discussions was the Defence, that may be as far as we get this week, in which case we'll have, perhaps, Witness AR on standby, just in case we finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the Defence confirm what the Prosecutor has just said? Do you agree? Mr. Krstan Simic, let us hear you. MR. K. SIMIC: Good morning, Your Honours. The Defence accepts the suggestion made by the Prosecutor and has no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojanovic maybe wishes to add something. Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is not an objection regarding the order of witnesses, but one of the last witnesses does not fulfil conditions to be heard this week. The Prosecutor can put him somewhere in the order of witnesses. We do not object to the order itself; however, we're going to raise an objection regarding the conditions for his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojanovic, you may discuss the issue with the Prosecutor, and afterwards you can bring up the issue in the courtroom. The witness is already here in the courtroom, and I really am not in favour of discussing similar issues in the presence of witnesses. 2

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. Have you had a good rest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good. We will continue with your testimony. Without much further ado, let me give the floor to Mr. Waidyaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. On Friday, Your Honour, when the witness testified, we were in private session. So now she would now testify in public, in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. We are in public session. You may proceed, Mr. Waidyaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. Examined by Mr. Waidyaratne: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, last Friday, I asked you whether you knew a person by the name of Miroslav Kvocka, and you said, "yes." How did you know him?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Miroslav Kvocka from way before. He was the brother of my colleague, Dragojla Kvocka who used to work with me at the court. I also knew him while I worked at the Prijedor police station. I would see him from time to time in the SUP. He was working there. So I know him very well. And his wife used to work with my husband. The two of us grew up together, and we used to be neighbours. We're very close, and I know when she married Miroslav Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the wife of Mr. Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know. Jasminka Crnalic. Her maiden name was Crnalic that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were in the Omarska camp, did you see Mr. Kvocka, Miroslav Kvocka, in the camp?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him several times in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court as to when the specific instances that you saw Mr. Kvocka, if you could recall?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember seeing him once when he entered the kitchen together with a group of people who were there with him, and he brought in a package, a parcel. I can't remember who else was with him, but I think that on that day, Radenko Stakic came with him. Radenko Stakic was the only SUP employee who approached me, talked to me a little in the room. So I cannot say with certainty that he was there on that day with Miroslav. This is merely my assumption.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when you saw Mr. Kvocka, how was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he was wearing a pair of trousers, police uniform. I believe it was a camouflage uniform. And he had a shirt with short sleeves. I cannot remember the details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I think that he was wearing at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you leave Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left on the 6th of August, sometime in the morning, around half past eight, 9.00. I went to the Trnopolje camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember this date? Do you remember how it happened?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we came to the restaurant that morning, we were ordered to clean the windows and to tidy up the dining area because they were expecting a visit from some journalists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody from the camp, who was in authority, come and tell you, inform you that you were going anywhere?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Meakic Zeljko came at that point. Actually, a bus with investigators had arrived, and Zeljko Meakic came, together with a man whose name I cannot her. And they told us, "You women are going home." We gathered around them, and they were reading out the names of those who were supposed to go home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, who was reading the names and could you describe this man who came with Meakic that day?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. It was a rather short man, an elderly man with dark complexion and dark hair. I had seen him in the camp prior to that. I also knew him from before, from the SUP. He was an employee of the crime department, and I think that he worked with Travancic, in the same office, and that he actually retired. But he was the one who was reading out the names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what was -- how did he read out the names? Did he have a list with him?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was holding a piece of paper in his hand, and as he was rather short, we were able to see, those of us who were around him. I was standing next to him, and I could exactly see the names. I could see my name, but he didn't read out my name while he was reading, only my colleagues. At one point I heard Velida when she said, "Next to my name there is a minus sign and not a plus sign. I'm staying here." Then she started to cry. Actually, she wasn't crying, but she was just silent. So I was expecting my name to be read out, and indeed my name was the last one to be read out. At that point I turned to Zeljko and I asked him what would happen with my husband. He told me he would also be coming to the Trnopolje camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you leave the camp that day? Were you taken to some other place?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were taken to Trnopolje. Trnopolje, that was reception centre, sort of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With regard to the person whom you mentioned by the name of Velida, who was she? Was she a detainee who was there with you, and to which ethnicity did she belong to?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Velida was detained with us, and she was Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember her surname?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I hadn't met Velida before. I knew her from the camp. I just know she was a teacher of history. On one occasion a guard went up to her and said, "Teacher, do you remember when you gave me a minus in history?" And he started to harass her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This Velida, was she left behind in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she stayed behind in Omarksa, and with her was Mugbila Besirevic, a relative of mine, also Esma from the Crvene Ruze. But to be quite sincere, I didn't pay much attention because I wanted to see where my husband was. I managed to catch sight of him and to leave him some food that I had on me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, have you heard about Velida or Mugbila Besirevic since or after you left the camp?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never heard anything about them, and they have not appeared in these past eight years. I think that the people who stayed behind in the camp know best what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned about a person who came into your room with Meakic the day that you left the camp. You said that he's the person that worked in the SUP and who was the inspector. Did you know his name while you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion, Fikreta mentioned his name, but I later forgot it, and I couldn't remember the name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in your testimony, you testified about a person by the name of Krkan, whose surname you knew as Radic, a person whom you had known previously.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Though years have past and the people and circumstances have changed, if you see that person today, are you in a position to identify him?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please look around the court, the people inside, and see whether you see this person. If you need, you can get up from your seat or if you want anybody to get up to see them clearly, you can make that request. Please look around court and see if you could identify this person. If you need, you can get up.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first person on my left with a yellow-check tie. He's changed a little. He's lost weight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell as to where this person is seated? Who is he? What's his name?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is seated -- he's first from the left. His name is Krkan, his surname, Radic. I don't know his first name, but his nickname was Krkan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say that he's the first person from the left. Is it from the door on the left side? And which place from the guard, could you tell?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In relation to the guard, he's on his right, and the way I'm looking, on the left. So he's the first person next to the guard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you kindly tell the row where he's seated? Which row is he seated in?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's seated in the last row, next to the wall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: May the court record reflect that the accused Radic has been identified by the witness. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned about a person, a retired person, inspector, and gave some other details, a short person. If you see this person today, if he's present in court, will you be able to identify him?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Though circumstances and people have changed, please look at the people. If you need, you can get up or even get the people whom you want to identify to stand up. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That man is not seated here. I do not see him in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, from Trnopolje, how long did you stay in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About three days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke about another person by the name of Miroslav Kvocka. I'm sorry that I couldn't ask this question before this. A person by the name of Miroslav Kvocka. Do you think if you see him today that you will be able to identify him?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please look at the people, the persons who are present in court, and see if you could identify Mr. Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Miroslav Kvocka is sitting next to Krkan, in the middle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How is he dressed?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He has a blue jacket and a light blue shirt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which row is he in?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the last row next to the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: May the court record reflect that the witness has identified Miroslav Kvocka. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. From Trnopolje -- you said that you were there for three days. Where did you go after you were released?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the place should be redacted. Thank you, Your Honour. That concludes the examination-in-chief. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Waidyaratne. Mr. Krstan Simic, what is the order for the cross-examination, please? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, only I and Mr. Fila will cross-examine this witness. The other Defence counsel have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic. You may begin. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. K. Simic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Fazlic.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've already heard my name. My name is Krstan Simic, and together with Mr. Branko Lukic, we represent Mr. Kvocka. I only have a few questions for you, and they will not take long. You frequently mentioned Mr. Meakic.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know him from before?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Mr. Meakic?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean before the camp?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, before the camp.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was chief of police in Omarska. Anyway, he was a policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. During your stay in Omarska, there were many colleagues of yours, investigators there. Among them was Ranko Mijic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not remember seeing Ranko Mijic in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember any of the investigators? Which one?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember Obrad Despotovic, Zarko Zec, Ilija Bilic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. During your stay, did you ever see Mr. Meakic issuing orders to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also during your testimony, you mentioned Mr. Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you knew him well and we don't doubt that. Before this testimony, did you have any contact with representatives of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you give a statement on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to the information we have, this was at the end of January last year; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you made that statement, did you tell the investigator everything that you could recall at the time?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I told them what I knew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in January 1999, you knew Mr. Kvocka well.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you telling the truth at the time?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I am telling the truth now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Fazlic, could you tell me, please, whether the statement you made then to the investigator, that is, to Mr. Keegan, was it read out to you?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was read out to me via the computer, because there was a failure and it couldn't print it out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you sign your statement?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on that occasion, you described a person you knew extremely well, that is, Mr. Miroslav Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, could you get closer to the microphone, please, because the interpreters are having some difficulty in hearing you. Thank you very much. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Could I ask the usher to show Mrs. Fazlic her statement in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Fazlic, please look at page number 6. The fourth paragraph in the English version on page 6. You were talking about Mr. Kvocka, a man you knew very well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will have to quote your answers: "I never saw Kvocka in Omarska." Then I am continuing to quote: "Most of the guards were from Omarska. I didn't see anyone I knew from Prijedor except for the inspectors."

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a mistake in the interpretation, because we always had a translator who was translating my statement. He made a mistake there. I did say that the guards were mostly from Omarska because no active-duty policeman was a ordinary guard down there in those premises. That would mean I don't even know Krkan, according to this interpretation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please avoid making any comments. I'm just showing you your statement. So you're saying it's a misinterpretation?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Probably a mistake must have been made in the process of translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In today's testimony, you said that you would see Mr. Kvocka in Omarska. Was he working there? Would he come on a visit?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him once as if he was looking for someone. I don't know whether he was on a visit or whether he was working there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is whether you saw him working in Omarska while you were there.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean under "work."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To be on duty.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see him being on duty. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions for Mrs. Fazlic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Fazlic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Simic. Mr. Fila. Yes, Mr. Fila. You have the floor, please. Cross-examined by Mr. Fila:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Fazlic. I'm attorney Toma Fila from Belgrade, and together with Zoran Jovanovic, I am Defence counsel for Mr. Krkan. And I'm not going to claim that you didn't see him. Could you tell us something about the purpose of that largest room on the first floor?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The largest room. I really don't know what its purpose was, what it was used for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, in which period of time were the inspectors upstairs?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would stay there from 7.30, when they arrived, until the afternoon, 5.00, half past five, when they left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we infer from that that there were no further investigations after that time?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there weren't any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So while you were sleeping, the rooms you were sleeping in, there were no interrogations?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no inspectors to interrogate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm talking about inspectors only.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were none.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now go into closed session, or should I formulate my question in such a way that it cannot be fully fathomed? I can do it either way, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I prefer to allow you to have a private session, otherwise, you're going to say that you were not able to ask your question. So please proceed, but just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we are back in open session. Mr. Waidyaratne, do you have any additional questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is Mr. Jovan Simic? If the Defence have concluded, I have no re-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I think that Mr. Krstan Simic told me that it would be just Mr. Krstan Simic and Mr. Fila who would be cross-examining the witness. But in any event, let us check. Mr. Jovan Simic, do you have any cross-examination for this witness? Mr. Jovan Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] No, that is correct. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] No, we have no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: No re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We know that Mr. Waidyaratne has no re-examination. Judge Fouad Riad, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mrs. Fazlic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I just want a few clarifications. You said when you arrived at the camp, Mr. Krkan asked you to go with him to give you some advice. Do you remember that? And tell you how to act in the camp.

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived at the camp, I didn't immediately see Krkan. I saw him only in the evening. In the evening, he came over to invite me to his office to register me, and that is when he advised me how to behave in the camp. He told me then not to talk with the other women too much, that there would be among them -- that there were women who had been armed. So he spoke to me in a friendly manner, as we had known one another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did he do that just as a friend or because he was one of the managers and people directing the camp, one of the influential people? What impression did that give you?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that as he was the most important person there that evening, he was shift leader, and that is what he told me. He introduced himself. That was the first part of the conversation, which was the formal part when he took down my name and all the other particulars. Then later on, we continued in a friendly tone because we had worked together for years in the same building. So this was an informal conversation that we had afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did he offer you any protection in particular, any special treatment?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. He didn't offer any special treatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was he the one who arranged your meeting with your husband or was it Meakic?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I approached Zeljko Meakic. I don't know whom Meakic had given orders to, but in any event, my husband came, escorted by a guard, who later on took him back. I don't know whether it was Krkan or Zeljko, but in any event, I asked Zeljko to bring him over so that he wouldn't be surprised to see me in the restaurant. Anyway, both of them were present, both Krkan and Zeljko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: They were present. Somebody was giving orders to the other, or were they on equal footing?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were all on an equal footing. I just know that when I made a request to Zeljko, he usually answered that request. I didn't address Krkan very much, only when he invited me over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Then I want to ask you something you just said this morning. When you left the camp, other women stayed, like Velida, Esma, and Mugbila Besirevic. So do you have an idea of why they stayed and why you left? What is the criterion of people who would stay and people who left?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I really don't know what the criteria were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And you never heard of them after that?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard that they were alive, that they reappeared anywhere. I later learned about Senka, that she appeared in Trnopolje later, and Esma from the Red Roses Restaurant, I heard about her. I can't remember her surname just now. I heard that she had left, but I never heard anything about Mugbila or Velida or Edna. She was in my room when she was taken away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You don't know if they are alive or dead?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that they are dead because surely they would have appeared somewhere in these past eight years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mentioned that when you arrived to the camp you said you saw many dead bodies, and you saw people being carried out, dragged out after the interrogations. Were there women among the dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were no women.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And among those who were dragged out, pulled out of there, as you said, of the interrogation, were there some women too or just only men?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only men, during the time I was in the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Riad. Madam Judge Wald tells me that she has no questions for the witness. As far as I'm concerned, I have only one question. Both parties have asked you a number of questions, Mrs. Fazlic. The Judges have also asked you some questions. But is there anything you, yourself, wish to say, something that has not been asked of you so far?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. You have just completed your testimony here. Thank you very much for coming to testify before the Tribunal, and let me wish you a safe journey back to your place of residence. Thank you very much, Mrs. Fazlic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, and goodbye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecution would call Mr. Kerim Mesanovic. And while we're waiting for the witness, Your Honour, there was one other additional matter with respect to the witnesses which I discussed with the Defence. Both Witnesses F and A have requested closed session proceedings instead of the confidentiality measures which they currently have been granted. The Defence had no objection to that request by the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic, Krstan Simic. Is it true? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have reached an agreement, and we do not have any objections to the protection of the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Witnesses F and A have requested a closed session. Let me consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Keegan, could you please give us the reasons for this request? Why have these witnesses changed their mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The change, as I understand it, has been requested due to the coverage that the trials now get, particularly within the former Yugoslavia, and in particular, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, where they have weekly shows. Again, much like the prior witness who testified in closed session, the very details of how they were brought to the camp, et cetera, will identify who they are, and in particular, Witness A has already had prior issues already which were discussed in the original motion, and both of them are greatly concerned that the reasons for which they've requested confidentiality to begin with will, in fact, still present a problem if not in closed session. And I'm not sure I can be much more clear than that unless we go into a private session now to discuss it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber will grant the protective measures as requested for Witnesses F and A.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mesanovic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: NEDZIJA FAZLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please read the solemn declaration that the usher is giving you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may now be seated. Make yourself comfortable. Could you come closer to the microphone a little, please. Thank you. You will first answer questions that will be put to you by Mr. Keegan, who is on his feet, on your right-hand side. Mr. Keegan, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Keegan:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, could you please advise the Court of your date of birth and your place of birth?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 25th of July, 1955, in the village of Laniste, the municipality of Kljuc, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you grow up?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I grew up in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's your educational background?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I completed a secondary technical school in Prijedor, and then I was further educated to become a computer programmer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do your compulsory military service?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you do that?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I did my military service in 1977 to 1978, in Tuzla, in the school for reserve officers. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were you trained to do as a military speciality?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I completed the school for reserve officers in infantry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, what is your ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your wife's ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: She's a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long have you been married?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: For almost 20 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you working prior to the beginning of the conflict in the Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I was working at the Secretariat of National Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in what section of the Secretariat of National Defence did you work at?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: In the section which was dealing with the mobilisation issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were your particular responsibilities within that section? What is it that you did?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Once an order for mobilisation is issued, I was in charge of decoding the orders. They would usually come coded. So that was what I was involved with. After the decoding process, I would forward the orders to the executive department so they could be implemented.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those decoded orders, as you referred to them, what would they actually contain? What was the actual result of that?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: They would contain the information as to which unit was in question. The name would be the war unit and then the number, so which unit was to be mobilised, which category of people, and what technical equipment was necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as part of the end product of your section, would you actually produce the lists of the individuals who were to be called for mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in 1991, who was the head of the Municipal Secretariat for National Defence?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Becir Medunjanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was the chief of the Mobilisation Department at that time?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Dzevad Habibovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was their ethnic background, if you know?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as you move into 1991, was there a change in the office personnel?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was that change?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The changes first occurred at the federal level. Territorial Defence committees were transformed into military organs, and there was an order to that effect coming from the federal level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the actual change that took place in the Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: In the Prijedor area, as those organs were formed, the units were supposed to be moved because the competency, the jurisdiction of the former organ, would remain at the level of simple instructions. As regards the organs, those who were involved in issuing orders were mostly Serbs. Not exclusively, but mostly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you refer to the organs that were changed, are you referring to the municipal committee from national defence being changed into something else?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was this new organ called?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Military territorial organs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that referred to by the acronym VTO?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you something about the request for mobilisations. Under the old system, when there were municipal secretariats for national defence, was it possible for a municipality to refuse to implement an order for mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the basis upon which they could refuse?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The basis for, for example, the economy being in danger, if the economy would come to a halt because of the number of people involved in a military exercise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with the change-over of the organs which you ever described, was there also a change in the way that mobilisation orders came to your department?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was that change?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Prior to 1991 and until the spring ever 1991, the orders would come from the federal level, passing through the republican level, all the way to the district of Banja Luka, which was the ultimate order-issuing organ as per municipalities. After the spring of 1991, the orders would bypass the authorities of Banja Luka and the authorities of the republic and the Federation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you referred to the orders coming from the federal level, does that mean that they originated from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And passing through the republican level, does that mean they went through the republican capital, in this case Sarajevo, for Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When do you recall the last regular mobilisation, that is, under that old system, occurring?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: In the spring of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thereafter, moving to the summer of 1991, where did you receive mobilisation requests from?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: In the summer of 1991, an order came which I saw with my own eyes. The Serbian republic, the Krajina of Knin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which of the republics of the former Yugoslavia is Knin located?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: In Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time, was that part of the self-declared Serbian republic?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the same time that these new military organs, the VTO, was being created, were there changes in personnel within the defence organisations in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were those changes?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: It was normal for the Mobilisation Department to be involved in that, and the VTO. Three people from the VTO, Muhamed Burazovic, Dzevad Habibovic and myself, we did not receive the approval, the permission to work within the VTO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why were the three of you not granted permission to work at the VTO, if you know?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The others were Serbs. So the conclusion would be that it was because we were Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you given an official reason from the VTO?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No. We were allegedly being checked, but we never started to work. I think that they're still continuing with their checks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "check," what do you mean? What type of check?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: An officer in charge for security should be involved in that. If we all spent over ten years working in that department, that means that that was not necessary. If others could be admitted without any checks, then the same should have applied to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this same time, were there changes in the command of the military barracks in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The former barracks commander, Colonel Muharem Efendic, was declared a homosexual, and he was forced to retire. And he was replaced by a Colonel or Lieutenant Colonel, I don't remember, Arsic. As regards the organizational and mobilisation department, Captain Radmilo Zeljaja was appointed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Efendic, what was his ethnic group, if you know?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Lieutenant Colonel Arsic, and Captain Zeljaja, what was their ethnic group, if you know?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, into the fall, through the fall of 1991, did you continue in your position as a programmer, preparing the mobilisation lists?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that time, the fall of 1991, were you requested by the VTO to prepare any particular mobilisation lists?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. The request was for a general mobilisation, but also a list of all Serbs was to be composed. So no code was used, such as the Yugoslav's. The only code that was used was 07, which referred to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now when you say the only code that was used, you mean that was the only personnel code that was directed on the mobilisation lists?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that only people with declared Serb nationality were then called up as a result of that mobilisation list?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because they didn't want to check the 42 code or category. The 42 code referred to Yugoslavs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as you moved into 1992, were there any further changes in the Mobilisation Unit with respect to how the records were dealt with and other issues?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, Captain Radmilo Zeljaja came with his escort to take over the complete database from the military department, that is, from the mobilisation affairs unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what, in effect, did that mean? Who now controlled the military records upon which mobilisations would be ordered?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The control over the military records was supposed to rest with the Municipal Secretariat, but unofficially it changed jurisdiction and came under the jurisdiction of the VTO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after the takeover in Prijedor on the 30th of April, 1992, were there further changes in the municipal organs related to national defence?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the morning of the 30th of April, the whole town was covered with their symbols, and a list of people who were able to enter the building was on the Secretariat, including the name of Becir Medunjanin, who was not allowed to enter the premises of the National Defence Secretariat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, I'm going to ask you, please, to slow down when giving your answers to give the interpreters a chance to hear everything that you say. Now, you indicated that Becir Medunjanin was not allowed to enter the premises. What about yourself and the other colleagues who worked with you in your office?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: We continued working until the 20th or maybe 22nd of May. I can't remember. Then we were told that we should no longer come to work because it was not necessary, there were no JNA-related instructions to that effect. That it was wartime, and that we should be on the so-called waiting list, and if necessary, they told us that we would be called up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the 30th of April, after Becir Medunjanin was not allowed to enter the building, was he replaced by anyone as the head of the Municipal Secretariat for National Defence?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 26th of April, 1992, a so-called assembly of the Serbian republic or the Serbian assembly, I don't remember the exact name, was established, and they had established parallel organs, including the Office of the Interior Affairs. They appointed their own person there. And the same happened with all major departments in the town, including the post office, the bank. The Serbian authority took over the key positions of power in the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was Becir Medunjanin replaced in the Secretariat of National Defence after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Becir Medunjanin was no longer allowed to enter the premises of the Secretariat, and he was replaced by Slavko Budimir. I don't know exactly who it was who selected him and appoint him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was Slavko Budimir's ethnic group, if you know?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Serbian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that you worked until approximately the 22nd of May.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicated that you were told that you should no longer come to work because it was not necessary. There were no JNA-related instructions. To your knowledge, did anyone continue to work in your section?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Even two retired former employees of the National Defence Secretariat were called up to replace the seven people who had been sacked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the ethnic group of those people who continued to work, including the two retired employees, if you know?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Serbian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the seven people who were sacked, as you put it, what was their ethnic group, if you know?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what, if any, events took place a day or two after you were told to no longer report to work?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The fear of moving around and the shelling started on the 23rd or the 24th of May. The areas involved were mainly Brdo, Banovic, and Rakovcani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time where were you living? What part of the area?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I lived in the centre of the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of the members of your office or the Municipal Secretariat of National Defence arrested on about 30 May?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Dzevad Habibovic and Muhamed Burazovic were arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where they were taken?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: They were taken to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at any time, were you called back to work in your office?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was that, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that it was a Monday, I'm sure it was a Monday. I don't know whether it was the 25th or the 26th of June. I was called by Spiro Marmat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were you told?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: He told me that I should appear for work tomorrow morning at 8.00, because they had changed the working hours in the meantime, and starting at 8.00. I apologise. I think it was on the 5th or on the 6th of June, not 25th or 26th of June, but the 5th or the 6th of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told why you were being called back to work?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't told anything, but in view of the nature of the work I was involved with, they didn't have anyone to replace me, and that was the reason why I was called back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if that would be a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. Keegan. I think we're now going to have a break. So let me first ask the usher to take the witness out of the courtroom. Half-hour break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that Mr. Lukic was taken Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. by surprise. Let me welcome the return of Mrs. Jelena Nikolic. We're going to resume the testimony of the witness now. You may be seated. Yes, Mr. Keegan. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, when we broke for the recess, we were talking about your return -- when you were called to return to your workplace in June of 1992.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you given any type of documentation or was any type of documentation necessary for you to be able to return to work?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that I used to work in the Secretariat for National Defence, they probably had permits for movement, and I received a similar such permit signed by the Secretariat for Internal Affairs, allowing me freedom of movement in town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the name of the person, if you can recall, who signed that freedom of movement document?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: On my permit, the name was Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you returned to work on that first day, how did you go to your office?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: As I had spoken to Spiro Marmat, who asked me to go back to work, as I had spent my childhood, my whole life in town and everyone knew me, and so I told him that he had to send someone to pick me up. And a driver came to pick me up, even though I was only four or five minutes away from my place of work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you feel it necessary to request him to send someone to pick you up?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Because I was afraid that somebody might stop me on the road in a drunken state and kill me. So that is why I asked to be driven to work, for reasons of my own safety.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once you were recalled to your office in June, for how long did you continue to work? Until what date?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I worked until the 24th of June, until 9.25 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened at that time?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I was getting ready to go home for breakfast when a policeman called Bato Kovacevic came up to me and told me that he wanted me for something. He led me to a green Mercedes with a police sign on it. He opened the right-hand door. He took out a document, a piece of paper, and read out my name, Kerim Mesanovic, father's name Fadil, I said, "Yes." He said, "They wanted you for something in Omarksa, but you'll be returned quickly." I asked him to let me go home to change, because I had heard from the Serbs what was happening. I had had summer clothes on, light-weight trousers and a T-shirt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you want to go home and change? What type of clothes did you want to change into?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Something warmer and that would be more suitable than what I was wearing. I think I had a white T-shirt on and very light trousers. I had no jacket. Also, I wanted to let my wife know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he allow you to go home?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No, because he said I might run away. Then I asked him to give me an escort. He gave me two policemen, one of them was Cvijic, and they drove me by car to my house. All this took five or six minutes. My daughter, who was then 13, was in front of the house. She didn't find anything unusual in this situation because it wasn't the first time for me to be accompanied by policemen, as we worked in the same building. However, when I left the building, policeman Cvijic handcuffed me and pushed me into the Mercedes in front of my daughter and to the cries of my wife, who pleaded with them, explaining that she was Serb, that I was innocent, that I had been working, that I had no plans to go anywhere. But it was all in vain. Cvijic just said, "If you don't shut up, you will go with him, you Muslim whore."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, you indicated you were accompanied by policemen on the way home before because you worked in the same building. Where was the offices of the Mobilisation Department located?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The department for mobilisation was in the SUP building. In the same building, therefore, as the police. We would have breakfast in the same room, have coffee together in the same room, take refreshments, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you were put back in the Mercedes by Cvijic, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: They took me in front of the SUP building. My former colleagues from work were looking from the window. I had a jacket over my hands and handcuffs, and they were asking me with their eyes where I was going. Then I showed them my handcuffs. Cvijic cursed at me and hit me at the back of the head, saying, "Why did you do that for?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you taken in the SUP building?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: They first took down my particulars. This was in the duty room. And the chief of staff of that room was Jovic. I think he had retired already before, but I'm not sure. He took off my handcuffs, and then the two policemen escorted me to a cell in the SUP courtyard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where in the SUP building complex are the cells located? Are they in the main building or in a building behind the main building?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: They are behind the main building, in the same courtyard. There's just one cell. Across the way was a large hall that was used for celebrations and meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was the canteen for the SUP also in that building behind, on the other side of the courtyard?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, upstairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was anyone else in that cell when you were placed in there?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: In the cell, Muharem Nezirevic, a journalist, was already there. And Davorin Zombra, the owner of a transport business. Aziz, I don't remember his name, an Albanian who had a confectioner's shop, a cake shop. Nihad Basic, who was the brother of one of the SDA officials in town, and some other young men whose names I cannot remember and whom I had never seen before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Muharem Nezirevic, what was his ethnic group, if you know?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Muharem Nezirevic, and all the others with the exception of this Albania and Davorin Zombra, who was a Croat, were all Muslims, myself included.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during the time that you were in that cell, were you beaten or otherwise mistreated?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: While we were in the cell, no one touched us or called us out or let us out until the evening, at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you taken out of the cell that evening?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That same evening, they called out names one by one, telling us to come out. We stood against the wall below the cell window, with our feet apart, with three fingers leaning against the wall. We were searched once again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you refer to leaning against the wall with three fingers, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Three fingers is, I suppose, their salute. Instead of saying, Zdravo, as we used to say to each other before, they would point their three fingers, thumb and the two fingers next to it. This was their salute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you please indicate or demonstrate for the Judges what you mean by that? Just sitting down.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: These were the three fingers, leaning against the wall, feet apart, wide apart, so that they could search us to make sure that we had nothing on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: For the record, the gesture that the witness used, used the thumb, the index finger, and the middle finger of each hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, were you directed to stand using that position or using that gesture to support yourself against the wall?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: We were told to lean against the wall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. My question is --

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during the time that you were searched, was anything taken from you?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: They couldn't take anything because I had nothing. It had been seized before I was taken to the cell, in the duty room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What had been seized from you?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: My lighter, two boxes of cigarettes called Vek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any identification or money with you?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were searched in the courtyard as you were leaning against the wall, were you beaten at that time?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They again called out, one by one, to enter a black Marija, a police van, the police van. And as I had my back turned, I heard the sound of blows. I don't know what was used to inflict those blows. Then Davorin Zombra was called out. The sounds were no longer just "tup-tup", but strong blows that went on for some time. There was no light because there were restrictions, so they used hand-held batteries. So as they called us out, I was told to run towards the car. And he lit up the police van. The light went off, and I felt a blow against my mouth. The upshot was that I lost four teeth. I fell to my knees, then came a blow in my back. I can't tell you whether I was kicked or a rifle butt was used or something like that, and I fell under the car as a result of that blow. From the direction of the door of the SUP building facing the courtyard, I heard laughter and words, "Hit the Ustasha," and swear words, cursing my mother, or "Hit the Mujahedin."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, did you know who the person who was hitting you -- did you know who that person was?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell what that person was wearing?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was dark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were hit in the mouth and your teeth were knocked out, do you know what you were hit with?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I assumed, and Zombra agreed with me -- he was very tall. He got a blow in the right eyebrow. He thought, and I did, that it must have been a karate expert. But there were many blows that covered my whole face.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were hit more than once, more than the one time that knocked your teeth out?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a blow in my back, and when I was lying down, I didn't count any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the van then took you to Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: They told us to get out in the opposite order. I was the first to get off. They pointed towards the wall, telling us to lean against it again, and to take up our position, which meant facing the wall, and we did. Then somebody ordered, "Search them." Then we heard a voice saying, "There's no need. They were searched this morning in SUP, so they're clean. There's no need to search them."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mesanovic, what building in the camp was this wall that you were told to lean against, on what building?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: As I was not familiar with Omarksa from before, that is, the mine. I later saw where it was. It was to the right of the entrance to the administrative building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after the individual said there was no need to search you, where were you directed to go?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: He told me immediately to turn around. He used military commands, which he didn't know very well. He said, "Turn to the left," and I ran towards the building, but he used the wrong command. I should have turned to the right. Then he told me to run towards the fire. And it was -- the building next to it was first called the shock building, and later it came to be call the "white house." The fire was burning in front of the "white house," probably to keep them warm. So I ran into that building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What room did you go into once you entered the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody told me which room to go into. However, as I was at the front of the column, I looked into the room to the left, but there were too many people there. If we had joined them, the eight of us, it would have been too crowded. Then I tried the second room to the left. It was even more crowded; the door couldn't be opened. Then the room in the middle was empty except for a man and a woman. I don't know why I didn't go into that room. Then I heard somebody shout behind me, "To the right," so I entered the room to the right. Later, we counted up the number of people inside. There were 45 of us in a room that was not bigger than 20 square metres, and the eight of us made it 53.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mesanovic, you indicated you went into a room on the right. Was that the first room or the second room on the right?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: From the entrance, it was the second room to the right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what was the condition of these prisoners who were already in that room when you entered?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: A condition that even medical people could not properly describe. Their faces were distorted; they were bloodstained. I recognised only one of them, that is, Bahrija Foric, who lived in the village in which my late father was a teacher. He was lying, and as he was the oldest man there, I thought that he was privileged. But, however, that was not true. He said he felt so bad, as if one kidney had been injured badly, and all he could say is, "What are you doing here?" There wasn't much conversation because we were not allowed to talk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in addition to the condition of the prisoners, did you notice whether there was blood anywhere else in the room?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The walls of the room I was in had been painted white sometime, and the ceilings were panelled in wood, but they were sprinkled with blood. And if you were to kneel, if you were to kneel down, then the stains would be at the level of your eyes, and I wondered why. However, the next evening I learnt from the men who had been there longer than me that the worst shift was coming, and they had promised them a party. The party --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. First I want to talk about that first evening. On the first evening, were prisoners in that room that you were in beaten?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what type of beating took place?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The beating consisted of blows with fists, kicks, rifle butts or barrels. It depended. The objects were not those used by professionals because after leaving the camp, I discovered that what professionals used were truncheons and that they're not so bad, but wooden and metal sticks are much worse and cause more pain. In any event, they used all kinds of things to beat us with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did they beat you, what part of the body?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Going from the head, arms, lower extremities. There was no rule. I even wondered whether perhaps they were all familiar with anatomy because people beaten to death had bruises mostly in the area of the heart and in the area of the kidneys where these bruises were darkest, which meant that that is where they beat most in cases when they decided to beat someone to death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you recognise any of the guards or any of the individuals who came into the room and beat prisoners on that evening?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next day, were you allowed out of that room or out of the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: We were allowed to go out for lunch, those wonderful 40 seconds that the lunch lasted. We had to run to the restaurant. And they would also take people out to go to the toilet in groups of ten during the day, if they felt like it, but mostly the whole thing would end up in a small jerrycan where people went to relieve themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there a reason why people didn't want to go out to go to the toilet?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The most important reason was first of all, you had to ask the guard who was at the door to go out; and then secondly, people had already learned from experience, those who went out would usually be beaten up and would never reach their destination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, earlier you referred to guards coming in that second evening to throw a party for the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: That is what I was told by the people that I found in that room. They told me that there would be a party, and they said, "You shouldn't have come yesterday evening. This is the worst shift." The party consisted in taking up certain positions, and that explained to me the traces of blood at the level of our heads. They were supposed to kneel down and put their hands behind the back and lean with their foreheads against the wall. That's what we all had to do. We had to come to the wall, and the guards would enter the room, and then the beating would start. It mostly consisted of blows in the head, inflicting all kinds of fractures and bruises. Two young men were hit, were injured in the ankle Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. because they would jump on them. So that is the kind of party they had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Referring to these two young men who were injured in the ankle, what do you mean "they jumped on them"?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, probably due to the position they were. They were -- they had their backs turned towards them. So probably one of them jumped on their feet or kicked them, hit them with the rifle butts, and this is how they received their injuries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Just so that we can make the record clear, you're referring to "them" and "they." We have to clarify who "them" and "they" are. The prisoners were kneeling down facing the wall with their forehead against the wall?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did that include those two young men? They were also kneeling down with their forehead against the wall?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, who jumped on those young men's ankles, if you know?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The guards. I don't know their names. I don't know their faces. The guards who were in charge of the "white house," or people who would come to the "white house" from other places: from the hangar, the restaurant, or from the pista.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you able to determine or did you become aware of what type of injury those two young men suffered with respect to their ankle?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Whether those were fractures or just sprained ankles, I don't know because they disappeared after several days. They didn't go out for lunch; they remained in the room. Not only them. Foric was also the one who stayed inside. They never went out for lunch. So they had probably sustained either fractures or sprain injuries. I'm not an expert. I wouldn't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they able to walk after that beating and after they sustained the injuries to their ankles, walk on their own?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned Bahrija Foric again. Do you know what happened to Bahrija Foric?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
