utterances.text: All of them, 43 people who were there because those eight were later on taken for interrogations and distributed elsewhere -- to the pista, I myself went to the glass area, and some of them went to the hangar -- but the 43 had allegedly been captured at Benkovac. That was the accusation. Apparently they had been armed and engaged in combat. And there was another young man from Tuzla by the name of Softic or Sivac, I don't know. He was the 44th one. And they were allegedly taken for an exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as far as you're aware, Bahrija Foric left the camp?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during the time that you spent in the "white house," did you recognise any of the other prisoners who were there within the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who were those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: In the small room to the left-hand side there was Azur Jakupovic, then Hajra whose surname I don't know. Darko was also there. I'm sorry,

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: and he was the only one I knew. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you recall -- okay. You referred to the small room on the left-hand side, and you mentioned Azur Jakupovic and then these others, Hajra and Anes. Were they in that same room?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Hajra, who was Hajra?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: According to what the detainees told me, I think she was Darko's girlfriend, who was a Serb by ethnic background. I don't know why he had been captured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was a Serb, Darko?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Darko, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what condition were those prisoners in: Azur Jakupovic, Anes Medunjanin, and Hajra?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Anes Medunjanin was in the worst condition, but Azur Jakupovic had gunshot wounds on both knees. I don't know whether it was a result of shooting or not. Hajra had also been beaten up but not as severely as Anes and Azur Jakupovic, and Ado Ekinovic as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Anes Medunjanin look like?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: On his left or right shoulder -- I don't remember exactly --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have any noticeable injuries on any other part of his body (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All those who were there had faces that had been beaten up, had fractures on their face, fractured jaw bones, for example, split lips, lips split open, and similar injuries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did that room look like, that first room on the left, that you could notice?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, just like any other room: It was covered in blood. The walls were covered in blood, which means that the beatings took place inside, not on the outside, in the presence of all who were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you were in the "white house," were you ever asked to carry anybody out of that building?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Thursday evening, the 25th going to the 26th -- but nobody had a watch, so I can't tell you whether it was before midnight or after midnight -- Eso Sadikovic, who was in the first room on the right-hand side, he was there together with Mehmedalija Sarajlic, who was the former president of the executive council. He, Eso, opened the door, and he said, "I need three men. One of our colleagues got sick." Well, I was sure that it wouldn't happen to me. I mean, I don't know, because Eso was a physician who used to work for the United Nations. So I went out, together with two other young men, and followed Eso. Mehmedalija Sarajlic was lying down on the floor. He was one of the members of the management board of the mine company and a member of the executive council of the Prijedor municipality. He had been beaten to death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I know that because his face was completely distorted. Mehmedalija Sarajlic had a very large head. Now, it sounds funny, but it was really a big head, and greyish hair. But you couldn't recognise his face. His face was completely smashed, and the lower part of his body was all covered in blood, and it was stinking. He had probably relieved himself during the beating. So we took him by his feet. I took his right foot and Dr. Eso Sadikovic by his left foot, and two other young men took him by his arms. A guard came to us -- I don't know his name -- and he was holding his rifle in the form of a cross or something to that effect, and he was singing this song called "Sveta Je Pamjat." I believe that it is a religious text that is usually read during an Orthodox mass. He was walking ahead of us, and we took him to the location which we referred to as Birek [phoen]. It consisted of a high wooden pole which was near the metal fence which was around the house that we called the "red house," and this is where we left Mehmedalija Sarajlic. At that point, then the guards told us that we can go and wash our hands and drink some water, which was sort of intimidating to me, but since I was with Dr. Eso, whom I had known since my childhood, I was convinced that nothing would happened to us. So we washed our hands, drank some water, and went back to the "white house."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the guard told you, you could wash your hands and drink some water, why did that intimidate you? What were you afraid of?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, from the stories that I heard when I arrived, because there were more than 43 people in the room, they told me that when they would ask to go to the toilet and to drink some water, many of them didn't return after that. People were afraid of dying all the time; every minute, every second.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long ask you spend in the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Three days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how is it that you were able to leave the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Dysentery appeared, and the guards were probably afraid for themselves and their families. We were taken to the toilet because they wanted to fumigate the place where we were staying. So they brought us to the toilet. There was one guard, the only one whom I remember from the "white house," whose name was Bajo. Actually, that is how we called him, because he would address us as Bajo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. What building were you taken to? Where was this toilet?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: It was in the hangar building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened when you were going into this toilet?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: We went there in groups of ten. When we got there, when we got to the toilet, we realised that it was all blocked and clogged, and the thing was all over the place, and I didn't want to get in because I had no place to wash myself. I took off my sneakers and put them in my jacket pocket. And then at that moment, Bajo, whose real name I don't know, only his nickname, Bajo told me, "That's very smart of you. It's much easier to wipe off feet than to wash sneakers." I wanted half a cigarette that he was smoking, and then he gave me a whole cigarette. And somehow I felt that he would be willing to help me. And I asked him whether he by any chance knew a policeman by the name of Zeljko Meakic, and he said, "Yes. He's a chief there. He's a boss. How do you know him?" So I told him about our family relations. I told him about my only brother and his relation with Zeljko Meakic. My brother married the sister -- that is, the daughter of Zeljko's uncle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you ask the guard if he would advise Meakic that you were there?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I asked him, and he did it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you later have a meeting with Zeljko Meakic?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was that meeting held?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: In the administration building, the administration building on the upper floor, the second room to the right, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you say to Zeljko when you met him in that office?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I was convinced that my troubles would come to an end, that that was it, that I had spent three days there and that that would be the end of the story, because I believed that someone would guarantee for me because I knew that I wasn't guilty of anything, that I had not taken part in anything whatsoever. And he asked me where I was. I told him I was in the "white house." And he asked me whether I had any belongings with me, and I told him that I had left my blazer and my sneakers in front of the "white house" during the fumigation. And he said, "No problem. Let us go back and pick those things, and I will move you to the glass area." At that point I really didn't understand what was going on because I was convinced that I would be sent home within five or ten minutes, if nothing because of our family relations. However, no. I stayed there. I stayed in the glass area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you specifically ask Meakic if he was going to arrange for you to be released, if he would send you home?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No. To be frank, I was petrified. I was frightened. I was afraid of him as well because it appeared that I was not going home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Meakic at any time tell you why you had to stay in the camp?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No. He told me that we were prisoners of war. He said it a couple of times. But he spoke in general terms, referring to us as prisoners of war, so I probably fit within that description.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you why he was moving you to the "glass house"?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Allegedly that was the most he could do for me because the "glass house" was under his jurisdiction and his personal protection. So -- well, when I got there, I found a number of young men who had been at the front line fighting the Serbs. I also found some people, former employees of the SUP there, and this is how I ended up in that group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that -- well, the English translation says that in the "glass house" you found a number of young men who had been "at the front line fighting the Serbs." Had those men fought against the Serbs at the front line?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No. They were on the front line in Croatia, in Vukovar, together with Serbs. Some were members of the former JNA that were engaged in combat in Vukovar. There were some reservists who had been in the area of Pakrac and Lipik as part of the research contingent, and some others whom I could name who probably were on friendly terms with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So those men who had been part of the JNA or the other reserve forces, they had fought with the Serbs, on behalf of the Serbs, against the Croats?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Meakic in fact move you to the "glass house" on that day?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you interrogated while you were in the Omarksa camp?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you recall when that was?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: It was on a Friday, the following week. I believe the following Friday in the morning hours. I was called out and taken upstairs. I believe it was the second door to the left. The interrogator was Ratko Milosavljevic, a so-called investigator, inspector, but he was not a professional one. He had worked in the forestry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other inspectors or interrogators in the room as well?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Together with him, sitting in the room, was Nenad Lakic, called Neso. He was a professional.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall anybody else?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: After a while, Nenad Lakic, Neso, left the room where we were, and Ratko and I were left alone. Sometime later, Neso came in with Miroslav Zoric, also a so-called inspector, because he's an electrical engineer, actually. My wife used to work with him in the same building, and for a while they shared an office together. And he said, "Hi, Kerim, old man. How are you?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of questions --

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Not "my wife"; his wife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Zoric's wife --

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Zoric's wife used to work in the same building where I worked, and we shared the same room for a while.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you beaten during this interrogation?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Zoric asked me what I was doing there, and I replied. I told him I had been picked up by them. And at that point he slapped me, and he said, "You were not picked up by them. You were officially apprehended. Watch your language." And then he continued with questions, which were accompanied with blows, curses. My interrogation took 1 hour and 45 minutes in total.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What types of questions were you being asked?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I was accused for betraying a military secret, for taking electronic data to Zagreb for decoding. And allegedly, we had been given 100.000 German marks for that, Stjepan Maric and myself, Stjepan Maric who was an electrical engineer, a computer programmer, who used to work in the mine company, and later on he worked as a computer programmer for the municipality, in the town hall. Together with that charge, I was also accused for issuing permits to Serbs and asking -- and taking 300 German marks per permit. I was also accused of having a brother who worked in Germany since 1986, and allegedly he brought drugs which I then sold. So they were looking for the money.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the accusation that you had sold the electronic database for 100.000 marks, did they mention anything about Maric during the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: When I tried to explain to Zoric that that was nonsense, he told me that my friend had confirmed that and that I had the money, my brother and I, who worked in Germany, that all I had to do was to tell him about the location of the money. When I mentioned this friend of mine, the colleague of mine, he said, "Well, there are certain problems. He cannot walk. And even if we bring him to you, I don't think that he'll be able to speak." He was telling the truth because Stjepan Maric had been beaten to death on the previous night, and he failed to show up for lunch on the following day. I think that he passed away at that time, as a result of the beating. So all I could do was to tell him about the money, and he told me everything would be fine, I would be allowed to go home, that all I had to do was give him the money. I told him I didn't know anything about the money. Then he slapped me again, abused me verbally, cursing my mother. And as of that time, Milosavljevic didn't ask any questions. Neither did Neso. Miroslav Zoric was the only one who did the talking. He asked me a question concerning the individual who called me back to work, and I told him it had been Spiro Marmat. And he said, "What are you talking about? Spiro Marmat had been retired for two years." So he didn't believe me about him, although it was very easy to check about the man who was still employed there. Then he slapped me again, and then he asked me when I had started to work in the National Defence Secretariat, and I told him it was in 1979, and he told me that I had been appointed to that position on the order of a Muslim. Then I told him that it was Rajko Zigic who had deployed me, who was a secretary of the municipal committee of the Communist Party. And he said, "Are you blaming the dead guy? Do you have anyone alive to vouch for that?" Because this individual had died a natural death. Anyway, the whole conversation was unreal, the questions were unreal, and they were accompanied by slaps and blows. And at the end he told me, "You're at the right place here. If we need you, we'll call you back." So after 1 hour and 45 minutes, I left the room where the interrogation was taking place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, later, did you have an occasion to speak with Zeljko Meakic on that same day?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: He came that afternoon and told me that my statement was no good, that I should give another statement. I didn't know what he meant when he said it was no good. Then on Saturday or Sunday, his driver Brk told me that he had removed me from the list. I said, "What kind of list?" and he said, "The cold list." It probably meant being dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when Meakic came to you and told you to change the statement, that you should give another, did he insist on that? Did you, in fact, make another statement?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the interrogation, were the interrogators drinking anything?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Miroslav Zoric is known as an alcoholic in town. That day he arrived with a bottle of beer in his hand, to the room where I was in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was he drinking during the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak to Meakic on other occasions than the time you were detained in the camp?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He told me not to worry, that I was now safe. I have already said that this was under his protection. And in case I should need anything and he was not there, as I was in the "glass house," and this was the premises underneath the offices, he gave me four names whom I can refer to. The first name was Miroslav Kvocka; the second was Krkan. I didn't then know his name because he was known in town as Krkan, as a professional policeman. A few people called him by name. Then there was Krle, another nickname. I don't know his real name. And Ckalja, I don't know his name either. These were men -- Krkan, Krle, Ckalja were shift commanders. And Miroslav Kvocka, a professional policeman, like Krkan, whom I knew from before coming to the camp, I knew Krkan by sight as well, Kvocka was apparently his deputy. That is how he described him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated earlier that your office was located in the SUP building in Prijedor, the police station building. Had you seen any of the men whom you've just named prior to being in the Omarksa camp at the police building in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were Kvocka and Krkan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you see either of those two men during the time you were in Omarksa camp?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what Miroslav Kvocka looked like at that time when you saw him in the camp?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I saw him, what I remember most is that he had gloves without fingers. I don't know when he lost them. Then he had bulletproof pants, a black T-shirt; on the right hand, a pistol, and in his hand, the pump-action gun; without a cap and without any insignia on his shoulders to indicate membership of any police or army units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could you describe again, please, what type of clothing he was wearing? Just the clothing.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Camouflage pants and a black T-shirt with short sleeves. That is what I remember best.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how tall he was?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Taller than me. I'm just under 180 centimetres, and he's over 180.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of build does he have?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Well built, a young man. He wasn't a bodybuilder, but he was well built. He was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The colour of his hair, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I always had problems remembering those things. I think darkish hair, going on black.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Krkan?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Krkan most frequently wore a police camouflage uniform. I can't remember exactly how many yellow stripes he had on his shoulder, epaulettes, two or three. When he was amongst us, he carried a pistol and an automatic rifle as component parts of his uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How tall was he approximately, if you know?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I think he was lower but a bit heavier. He had quite a big stomach. He was on the fat side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how often did you see these men in the camp?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Very often. I didn't see them every day, but very frequently. Whenever they were on duty. Almost every time they were on duty, because I was in the "glass house," so that I could watch the handing over of duty by the guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see both of these men throughout the entire time you were in the camp? In other words, did they remain in the camp the entire time you stayed there?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't see Kvocka all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when it was that you noticed he was not in the camp any more?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was the first half of July. Towards the end of the first half of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware if anyone replaced him?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was that person, if you know?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: A retired professional crime technician, Drago Prcac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Because I knew him personally. Not just by sight. We would greet each other by name, because he was extremely close to our mutual colleague, Muhamed Burazovic, who disappeared while Prcac was working there. And because the witness at my wedding also worked with Prcac. His name was Zivko Radulovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Drago Prcac when he was in the camp?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What function, if any, did he -- or what position, if any, did he hold in the camp, that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: He came to replace Miroslav Kvocka, because Kvocka was dismissed. He brought his brothers-in-law, and that is how we knew that Kvocka had been replaced by Drago Prcac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned two other shift commanders, Ckalja and Krle. Did you have occasion to see those individuals in the Omarksa camp?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you known either one of them prior to being in the camp?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you learn their identity when you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: We could hear the guards addressing one another, or when the prisoners were talking they would hear one being called Krle, the other Ckalja, and that is how I learnt their names. Also, I already mentioned Zeljko Meakic had told me to address them in case I were to be called out, and he gave me the names Krkan, Krle, and Ckalja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time you were in the camp, did you ever have an occasion to speak directly with any of those three shift commanders?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was that, and when?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Krle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you have to speak to him?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the date, but I know it was a Monday. The 27th of July, when Dr. Begic, a surgeon, and Krle, I claim, and Krle knows that, he tried to protect him from everything, because apparently Dr. Begic had helped his mother or something like that. That day when Krle came on duty, Begic was not around. The previous shift was Krkan's. Begic had been taken in the direction of the "white house." Then Krle came and called me to ask me where Begic was. I said that he had left in the direction of the "white house." He cursed and turned around. He probably wasn't glad to hear this about Dr. Begic. And that was the end of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you recall what Krle looked like at that time in the camp? Can you describe him?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll try. He sometimes wore camouflage and sometimes olive-grey trousers. Also, he sometimes wore a civilian T-shirt, sometimes a short-sleeved shirt because it was summer. He had a receding hairline. He's a bit taller than me. He has darker hair than me. On one hand he has a tattoo of three hearts in a chain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, the translation said -- the English translation said he has a tattoo on his hand of three hearts in a chain.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: On his lower arm, three hearts, one following another. I can't remember whether it was his left or right arm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How is it that you know about this tattoo?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Because it was visible. T-shirts had short sleeves. In the former Yugoslavia, young men would wear tattoos when they went to the JNA or when they left the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether there was any writing within this tattoo or as part of the tattoo?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: In the hearts, I'm not quite sure, there was "I," "You," and "We." About the "We," I'm not quite sure, but I know there was "I" in one of the hearts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, earlier you spoke about the date of your interrogation, the Friday. Was that day referred to by any particular name by the prisoners afterwards? Did it come to be called something?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was Black Friday. That's how we called it. Because when going for lunch, every group was beaten, and coming out from lunch, every group was beaten. The corridor was prepared for people going in. They poured some detergent on the floor for washing dishes. Then they put trays on that, on top of that. They stood between two cupboards. To the right when you enter the corridor there were the cupboards where the workers would undress, and they would stand there. To the left was a toilet and another room, and they would be standing on that side too, and they would form a kind of gauntlet, a welcoming committee. The first person to step on the tray would slip because of the detergent, and the rest of the 20 or 30 in the group would fall on top of this first or third or fifth person in line and then the beating would start. Then people would get up and go in for lunch, for which there was 30 to 40 seconds. You would pour the contents of a plate on the eighth of one loaf of bread, sometimes less. If the guard sees you doing it, he Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. would hit you on the hand. Then the piece of bread would fall from your hand. Then you would have to bend down, and he would hit you on the back, saying, "I'm feeding you, and you're throwing the food away." Then the people in charge of the restaurant, Milutin Popovic, known as Pop -- I learnt his name later on. In Omarksa he was known as Pop. He was together with Ranko, known as the electrician. I never saw either of them, him or Pop. The two of them would be the most prominent in this kind of mistreatment during lunch, and they were most to blame for this Black Friday. They were probably assisted by others, whom I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say you never saw either of them, him or Pop, do you mean you didn't known them from before you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, that's not what you mean, or no, you didn't know them from before?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know them from before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in addition to this -- first off, with respect to this day, this Black Friday, was there any kind of reason given by the guards or anyone else in the camp as to why these beatings were taking place that day, that you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Whether these were rumours amongst ourselves or rumours that leaked from them, the reasons were: If somebody was killed on the battle front fighting the Muslims or the Croats from his own village, they would use that as an excuse to take it out on us who were detained there. Or the reason could have been a religious holiday, after which they would celebrate until dawn, all night, and mistreat us. I don't know what other reasons they may have used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was referring to just that particular day. Do you recall for that specific day whether there was any reason given?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I think it was the 4th of July. In the former country, that used to be Veterans' Day. I cannot remember that there may have been any cause on that particular day. I don't think they even had any new prisoners that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in addition to that day, the Black Friday, were there other occasions when prisoners were beaten on their way to or from getting meals?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a daily occurrence. It would be rare for a whole group to go unscathed. They would get a blow regularly, except perhaps the last two days before the closing of the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you ever recall seeing any of the commanders or shift commanders whom you have referred to present when these beatings at mealtime occurred?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: It is very hard to tell because like the others, I would try to hide, not to be conspicuous. But if their shift was on duty, it is to be assumed that they knew and saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, why do you say it's assumed that they knew or saw?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Because I would see them occasionally, looking through the window. They would go outside on the roof where there was a machine-gun nest, in military terminology, facing the hangar and the pista and the "white house." There would be a guard there, and occasionally I would see them go out to this terrace or rooftop to see what was happening below. So they must have seen what was happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how often did interrogations take place in the camp?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: All six days in the week, including Saturdays. They would come at 8.00 and leave at 5.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the "glass house," were you able to hear anything from the interrogation rooms?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were directly above us, the interrogation rooms. As I said, I was in the first to the left, and then I don't know how many offices there were upstairs. The inspectors were there. If I were to try and give you the number, I could, but I think there were about 15 of them. They were interrogating, and they all were full, because there were people waiting in line. And these interrogations went on for some time. Sometimes they were shorter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of sounds would you hear from these interrogation rooms?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The sounds were most unpleasant to listen to. There was crying, begging, pleading. "Don't beat me. I haven't done anything. I didn't do anything. Brothers, don't do this." I remember one saying, "Brother, why are you beating me so?" And the answer was, "We're not brothers." Mainly moans, cries, sounds of pain. This went on almost all day, so that at one point I thought of leaving the "glass house" and going somewhere else. I just couldn't stand listening to it any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any occasion when you could hear the sounds of the actual blows?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, particularly when the people from the Brdo were brought in. One of the worst interrogators was Radak Knezevic, a retired professional. He interrogated these guys from Brdo, and he had three or four regular questions. "How tall are you? What do you weigh? What size shoes do you wear?" and, "Why do you curse my mother?" The blunt blows could be heard, and also the sound of metal against the table when they missed. And Rade would say, "Don't pay any attention to them. Talk to me. Pretend they're not there." And then again the same questions, "How tall are you? What do you weigh? What size shoes do you wear?" Those were the questions put by a professional, though I must say a retired professional.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any of the commanders or shift commanders that you referred to present in the area when these beatings were occurring during the interrogations?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, from the "glass house," were you able to see when new prisoners arrived at the camp?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Not always, but yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for those occasions that you could see this, what would happen when the prisoners arrived?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: If it was a small group of one or two men, they would come in passenger cars or in a police van. The guards who would be there would inflict a couple of blows. But when a larger group arrived -- I remember one group coming by bus from Keraterm -- they had to run the gauntlet to enter the "white house," and they were beaten. Whoever passed through this double row of guards would be beaten, beaten fiercely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you recall who would go to meet new arrivals, prisoners, as they came?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: In most cases, the shift commander and one of the guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what would they do, this shift commander and the guard who accompanied him, when the new prisoners came in?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Sometimes they would get some kind of a document or a piece of paper. Sometimes the guard would take them to a building. In most cases the "white house," because that's where the selection was done in preparation for interrogation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would the shift commander be present when the prisoners were being beaten, these new arrivals?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see a shift commander do anything to prevent the beatings or to stop the beatings?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing in particular. They would stop eventually, but I don't remember them doing anything in that sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, you referred to three shift commanders, Krkan, Krle, and Ckalja. Do you recall each of those shift commanders being present at one time or another when new arrivals came and were being beaten?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, would that be a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is welcome, but I was hoping you would finish the examination so we could have a break and then go on with the cross-examination. How much more time do you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Probably 20 minutes maximum, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. We're going to have a half-hour break. I'm going to ask the usher to accompany the witness out of the courtroom, please. A half-hour break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Very well then. I think we are now ready to continue. You may do so, Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, the commanders, shift commanders, that you've mentioned, Kvocka, Kos -- excuse me, Kvocka, Krkan, Krle, and Ckalja, did you ever see any of those individuals issue orders, give orders to guards in the camp?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That would happen when a gathering would form, and then they would disperse the group. Maybe if several people were at one particular point, for example, those who were in the restaurant but not were actually in charge of the restaurant, that they would be told to go elsewhere to their positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Once again, when you say a group would form, those who were in the restaurant but not actually in charge, who's "they"? Who is it that you're referring to who would form in groups?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The guards. The guards who came there. There were probably several of them. They were people who were in charge of the restaurant, and some were assigned to other places. They knew what their respective positions were, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who do you recall coming to these groups and telling them to return to their assigned locations?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: A shift commander would do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this happen on a fairly regular basis on each of the shifts?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The guards usually maintained their assigned positions?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Probably, because specific guards were assigned to specific positions, and we would see them when they were on duty, when their shift was on duty. So that meant that they were in charge of those locations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, did you ever see anyone killed during the time that you were in the Omarksa camp?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I learnt that the individual's name was Crnalic. I know his brother better. He used to play handball for the local handball club in Prijedor, but I don't recall his name. He was killed in the evening hours. It must have been before 7.00, because it was right before the change-over of the shift, and that his name was Crnalic. I learned that because people who were from his part of the town recognised him. So they told me that his name was Crnalic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was he when he was killed, where in the camp?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: He was on the left-hand side as you enter the "white house," but he was actually in front of the "white house." The door was on the left and there was a bench in front of the door, and he was sitting on that bench. Later on, people who had been with him told us that he had left the "white house" through the window and come to the bench to sit down. Some people said that he was a retarded young man. I don't know whether that was true or not. But it was probably very hot and that was the reason why he went out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, how was he killed?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The guard yelled at him, he told him to stop or something to that effect, but the poor guy, he stood up, and he went to the guard and fire was opened. The guard also opened fire, and he was killed on the spot. It was terrible to see, because he fell down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, do you remember whether any of the commanders or shift commanders you've mentioned were present when Crnalic was killed?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The left corner, in the direction of the "white house," there was an awning with chairs and tables underneath for the guards to take shelter in times of rain, and the commander of the camp was there and a shift commander, Krle, was also there. And when I say the "camp commander," I meant Zeljko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Zeljko Meakic?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see dead bodies in the camp, other than Crnalic?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Almost every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were those bodies usually placed? Where would you see them?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The bodies were on the corner between the "white house" and the "red house." Right next to the corner of the fence. And I told you about Mehmedalija Sarajlic. That was the location that I had taken Mehmedalija Sarajlic before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that be the grassy area that's to the left of the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any time, do you recall an occasion when there was an unusually large number, an extremely large number of dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. On that night, shooting occurred. I believe it was before the closing down of the Omarska camp and before a visit of some international TV stations. We heard shooting coming from the direction of the "white house." It was a very foggy night. I cannot remember the date, but it must have been the end of July. Not August, at any rate. The shooting was coming from the direction of the "white house." There was no electricity that night. Only the floodlights were on, which were using a power generator. So the floodlights were on, but we couldn't Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. see anything from the "glass house." We couldn't see what was happening over there. It was a very heavy, difficult night, and when it dawned, the fog started to disperse, and we heard noise of a truck coming from the outside, and at that point, you could see clearly how the bodies were being loaded onto a truck, but it was actually carried out with an excavator which belonged to the mine company before. So the bodies were loaded onto a truck with an excavator scoop. And they passed by the restaurant, so we could see the truck which was full of people. And it came back once again, loaded the people again and went off. Luckily, they didn't come back for the third time. But the "white house" was empty after that day. Everyone who had been there was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any estimates or any information as to how many bodies there may have been that morning?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Judging from what I could tell and from the number of people that were in while I was there, probably about a hundred people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, do you have any recollection of whose shift was on duty that evening, that is, when you heard all the shooting?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was Krkan's shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honour, I'd like to have the usher assist me, and have the witness just point out a couple of locations on the "white house," very quickly on the model, that he's referred to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, if you'd stand up. Could you put on this other set of headphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if you could take the roof off on the restaurant side. The other side. Just -- the other side. Just there so the Judges have a better view. That's it. Take that off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, first, Mr. Mesanovic, you've mentioned the "glass house" where you were kept. Can you point out where that is on the model?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The "glass house" is here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And it appears that on the model, the "glass house" had no roof on it. Was that, in fact, the case at the time you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. And when it rained, we had a shower. We could have a shower. Sometimes they would let us in into the restaurant to spend the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there parts of the "glass house" that were actually covered by an overhang of the roofs from the two sides of the building?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was a kind of awning. I don't know how big it was, maybe one metre, but it was not a real roof. It was a kind of awning. I don't know how else to call it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you referred to this terrace, this roof where the machine-gun was, where you saw shift commanders go out to see what was going on, for example, during the beatings at lunchtime. Could you point to where that roof terrace is where the machine-gun was?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Here, in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour, that would be the area of the lower level of the model of the administration building that's on the side next to the entranceway where the stairway is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can return to your seat, please, Mr. Mesanovic. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I'd like to now show the witness three photographs, Your Honour. They've been marked Exhibits 3/118, 3/119, and 3/120. The Defence have seen these exhibits before. We're endeavouring to get number of requisite copies to be made. We're waiting for them to come back from the outside. You can put that on the ELMO, please. The first picture is 3/118. If that could be placed on the ELMO, and could the ELMO be pulled back a little bit to get the full photo. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, have you seen this photograph before?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have, but only as a TV still. Actually, on TV, not as a photograph. I saw it as part of a video clip.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this the video -- part of the video that was shot by the international journalists when they came to Omarksa camp?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you recognise what it is that this photograph is depicting? Other than, obviously, the individuals, the prisoners who are in the foreground. But what we're looking at in the background there, can you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. This is the "glass house."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from where is this photograph being taken? In other words, where was the photographer standing when he took this photograph?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: In the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is the view from the restaurant into the "glass house"?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Corrects.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to recognise any of the individuals in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could point on the photograph on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Mirsad Dzohlagic, Dzevad Hadzibegovic my colleague from work, Serif Kadiric, a former policeman and driver at the Energo petrol company. Enes Suljanovic who owned a car repair workshop, and this should be me behind the pillar. This man here is Reuf Travancic, a former SUP employee. I know, but I cannot see now, but I know that Rizo Begovic sat next to him, but I cannot see him here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If we could put the next photograph, 3/119, on please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this photograph, do you recognise any of the individuals?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which one is you, please, if you could point on the ELMO. And this is also a photograph, a zoom-in of the people in the "glass house," including you. And who are those people next to you, to the left -- to the right, I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Serif Kadic, a former policeman, driver, with the Energo petrol company, Enes Suljanovic, a private entrepreneur who owned a car repair shop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And now photograph 3/120, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you recognise the individuals in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My colleague from work, Dzevad Hadzibegovic, his brother-in-law Mirsad Dzonlagic, and this man here is a deputy, a young man from Trnopolje. Mevludin was his name, Mevludin Sejmenovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This photograph is a close-up of an earlier photograph that you showed us where you pointed out your colleague Dzevad Hadzibegovic.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about the individuals that you can see behind them who appear to be sitting down. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. This here must be a driver from Kozarac. We used his jacket when we were taken for interrogation. It was a thick jacket, and we were in less pain as a result of that. This man here, sitting in trousers that were taken from one of the closets, was Nahid Besic, who was there from the 30th of May. And from what I can remember, this should be Beco Karanvic, who used to work in Cirkin Polje, at the centre for retarded children, school for retarded children, as we called it. This is what I can remember according to their seating positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, those men, would they be sitting under that area that was covered by a roof, where the overhang was? Is that the area that they're in?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall anybody else who used to sit in that area?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. There were quite a few of us. Mirso Kugic was there, Rizo Verbegovic, my aunt's son-in-law Ado Sadikovic who was killed around my birthday, Dr. Menso, who survived, Dr. Begic was there as well, who unfortunately did not survive. And the Crnalic brothers, Adnan, Nedzad, and Rizo, Rizah. Kvocka's brothers-in-law. They were there while Kvocka was deputy commander. I mean, they were not there while he was deputy commander, but after Kvocka had left -- I mean, he brought them back to the camp again. Reuf Travancic was there, Mile Mandic, a Serb, who owned a coffee shop, then Ismet Amolic, who worked for the work inspection organisation in Prijedor, and he was educated actually to become a Hodza.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, when did you leave the Omarksa camp?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of August, in the afternoon hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken from Omarksa?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I was taken together with a group of people to Trnopolje. A large group was taken to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you leave the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: It was a Thursday, the 6th of August. In the afternoon of the 6th. I don't remember the exact time. I didn't have a watch. And I arrived in Trnopolje on the same evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go from Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: From Trnopolje, I went home for 24 hours, and the following day I went back to the village where my brother lives with his wife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what --

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: To the village of his wife. Petrov Gaj, the birthplace of Zeljko Meakic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you stay in the area where the family -- Zeljko Meakic's family homes were, where his relatives lived?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it must have been around the 16th. At the beginning of the second half of September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how were you finally able to leave the area?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I had to leave, because in the meantime, a young man from Petrov Gaj was killed in the front line near Gradac, and the night before that, they had come to kill me. They had someone to replace the young man, the killed one. And I went to Prijedor in the evening, and I remained in Prijedor until -- it was on Wednesday, and I stayed in Prijedor until Friday, and on Saturday morning I left Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have to use a fake ID card in order to get out of the area?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had an ID which had been given to me by my sister-in-law from Novi Sad. The name was Zdravko Lukic, the actual name of the ID. I put on my photograph, and the seal read, "elementary school Donja Ljubija", instead of the SUP seal. And I was able to leave in a bus which was taking the local workers to Slovenia where they were working. I went to Novi Sad, and from Novi Sad I went to Germany. My brother came to pick me up and take me to Germany.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You used a Serbian identity in order to get out of the area.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to the time you were in Omarksa, did you know a man named Zoran Zigic?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you know him?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: We lived in the same neighborhood and we went to the same primary school. I even think he went to school with my brother. And I think that we both underwent surgery in Banja Luka in 1967. It happened so that we were there together. He will remember it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what he did prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: He was a taxi driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any time, did you see Zoran Zigic in the Omarksa camp?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any time, did you see him in the Trnopolje camp while you were there?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, do you recall being interviewed by members of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall being interviewed by members of the Tribunal's Office of the Prosecutor and being shown some photo boards?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall you were shown three photo boards?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that the only person you identified on any of the three photo boards was Zoran Zigic?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your testimony, you've referred to the three shift commanders who Meakic identified for you and who you saw in the camp, and Miroslav Kvocka as the first deputy commander and then Drago Prcac. And you've also referred to Zoran Zigic as a man you knew. I'd like you to look around the courtroom to see if you can identify any of those persons as being present here today. If you need to, you may stand up. And in looking at any person, if it would assist you to have someone stand up, you may make such a request. I'd ask you to identify the person by name and what they're wearing, please, if you can identify anyone.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Sitting at the first table is Zoran Zigic, the taxi driver. Behind him on the right-hand side is Krle, Krkan and Kvocka sitting in the middle. I can't see Drago Prcac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You may stand up if you want.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't see Drago Prcac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said Zoran Zigic is in the first row?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe what he is wearing, please?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: He's wearing, I believe, a dark blue coat, light shirt, and his tie has something yellow on it but it's mostly blue. He has a scar on his -- on the right side of his face.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Krle, you said he was behind him. Could you tell us what he's wearing, please?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Krle is behind him, yes. He's wearing a white shirt and a dark tie. I apologise. I cannot tell the exact colour. My eyes are tired. He has a grey blazer on, and he has a fringe on his forehead, and his parting is in the middle. Kvocka is sitting next to him. He's wearing a dark blue coat, a light blue shirt. Next to him is Krkan, who is wearing a burgundy shirt, and then green. I'm not sure about the nuance of the colour, and he has a striped shirt -- tie, I'm sorry .

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You may sit down, please. Mr. Mesanovic, is there any doubt in your mind that those three men, Krle, Kvocka, and Krkan, are the three men who you saw in the Omarksa camp?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour. I'm sorry, Your Honour. For the record, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If the record could record a positive identification of Zoran Zigic, Milojica Kos, Miroslav Kvocka, and Mladjo Radic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Keegan. Mr. Krstan Simic, in which order are you going to cross-examine, please? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence will cross-examine in the order of the indictment. We still are not sure whether all the attorneys will cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. So you will be the first one. You have the floor. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Please go ahead. You have the floor. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. K. Simic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, my name is Krstan Simic, and together with my colleague Branko Lukic, I represent Mr. Miroslav Kvocka. In the context of your testimony and the experiences you unfortunately went through, we will have a few questions for you. You said that you were brought to Omarksa in a van. How many policemen were escorting you and do you know any of them?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the number nor do I know any of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The policemen were sitting in front, were they?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because I was driven in a police van, in a Black Marija, and you were separated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From whom? From the driver?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you got off the first.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have to raise your arms and lean against the wall immediately?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as we got off, we were told, "Against the wall with your hands up."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was the same procedure applied to all?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had no handcuffs?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. During your testimony a moment ago when you were talking about the comments made by shift commanders, you said that the guards had particular guard posts where they kept guard; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Today you told us that you worked in the department for mobilisation in the Secretariat for National Defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that department carry out orders for mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There may be a misunderstanding. If I understood you correctly, the department did not make a decision on mobilisation but carried out the decision taken by someone else.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Secretariat for National Defence, a department of Prijedor, had data on all military conscripts in the Prijedor municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we talk about conscripts -- since you were professionally engaged in that area, can you describe what a conscript is?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: A person capable of serving in the army as a recruit, when he fulfils certain conditions, medical, psychological, he serves in the army. After doing his military service, he becomes a military conscript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Upon his return from military service in the JNA, that person is registered in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We already have him in our records. Even before he goes to the JNA, he is in our records. Files are established before people serve. It is on the basis of those records that we call up individuals for military service, who become recruits. Upon serving, completing their service, they become conscripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When a person has completed his military service, in your records, does he acquire a certain military assignment?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he does, depending on the needs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So every able-bodied person has a military assignment?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: In most cases. There were people -- there was a category of military conscripts who were not assigned to any position because they were working in Macedonia or Slovenia, because for them to come from Macedonia, they would need 24 hours. This would entail a great deal of expense. So we would not call up such people, at least not before this latest war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned this category of persons who were assigned to military posts or military units. Who were they?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: They are reserve military conscripts. People who had completed their military service in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, when your department receives instructions to carry out a mobilisation of military conscripts for the needs of a particular unit, what would be the department's duty?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The duty of the department would be to draw up call-up lists, to categorise them according to mobilisation positions and directions, then according to their addresses, to send them to mobilisation checkpoints. And there were 45 such mobilisation points in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Within the framework of this mobilisation procedure, were there military conscripts who, according to their military assignments, had what was known as a work obligation?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did that mean?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: That would mean that if they were mobilised, they would report for duty at workplaces or -- to their regular workplaces or wartime workplaces. For instance, if a large number of lawyers had been called up from a mine or from a company, then others would be given the work obligation to work there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Judges?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Judges did not have such wartime obligations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me put the question to you. We have a Judge whose work obligation in wartime is to work in court. In the event of mobilisation, where does that Judge report to?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: To the court. The place indicated in his military booklet. In this case, it would be the court, on the basis of his work obligation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about a policeman? Would he retain his work post?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the event of mobilisation, when people have to perform work obligation at their regular or special work posts, is that considered to be fulfillment of their duties under mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't have the opportunity to send people to do work obligation. We only covered the mobilisation to military units, not work obligation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me make my question simpler, please, Mr. Mesanovic. Under conditions of war, a policeman called Zeljko Meakic is mobilised. Prior to that, in your records, he has been assigned as a policeman. What is his duty once he receives call-up papers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Is this a conclusion from the counsel? Is he testifying here that Mr. Meakic was, in fact, mobilised, or is this a hypothetical? In which case, it should be posed as a question and not as a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic, your response? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] My response is that this is not a conclusion. We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's a hypothetical question. Is it a hypothetical question? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we're not here to learn about abstract matters. The witness should be asked specific questions. Do you have a question to put to the witness regarding Zeljko Meakic and his work obligation? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] I do. I do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed then. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] I shall rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, to simplify things, a person who is registered in the military records and who, on the basis of his wartime assignment, is assigned to his regular work post, in the event of mobilisation and the implementation of the order on mobilisation, where does that person report for duty?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the place he's assigned to as indicated in his military booklet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mesanovic, you also mentioned that materiel can also be mobilised on the basis of this mobilisation procedure.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Secretariat for National Defence, the Prijedor department, as we're talking about a municipal level, did it have in its records mobilised certain materiel and equipment for the needs of military units, the police, the Territorial Defence, and the like?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean an inventory of that equipment. Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did that mean?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: It meant that the state had at its disposal all materiel and equipment in the event of the threat of war or a war, that is, the state or the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The trucks of certain companies, would they also be covered by this mobilisation and assigned to certain positions?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about passenger vehicles?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, even horses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to the instruction for mobilisation, the owner or user of a certain object is obliged to bring those objects and that equipment to a certain place as indicated. And he already knows where he should bring those assets?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as he receives the document, it is indicated where to go. For persons, it was on a white call-up paper, and for resources and assets, a blue piece of paper which indicated where those assets should be brought to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When an owner delivers an asset of that kind, does he receive a receipt for it?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After delivering it.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the end of an exercise, a military exercise, are those assets returned to their owners?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is some kind of a report drawn up on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, a report on the technical properties, that it is in good working order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If any damage were to be inflicted on those assets, was the owner entitled to damages?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, do you really need all those details? Please continue. I'm just wondering whether you really need all those details about this particular question. But you are doing your job. It's up to you. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think you will see later on that I do need those details. But thank you anyway for your comments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, we're going back to your testimony now when you said that you were undergoing a security check. You remember that point in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. 1 Q. Military units of a higher level, did they have a security department?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the organigramme, did wartime units have a sector for security or a security officer?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for intelligence and security affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those activities within units, were they veiled in a certain degree of secrecy in view of the kind of activities they were?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A security and intelligence officer, were they answerable exclusively to the commander?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Probably. That is part of the military hierarchy of which I am not too familiar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the fact of the division between the army, the police, the administration, and so on, were there certain cases when the commander of the Kozarac police station could issue orders to a security officer in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Within the mobilisation procedure, was it possible for the army to be subordinated to the police?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I am not a military expert.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
